title: Modern Readers: Engaged, Reform and Convert Buddhism
bigQuestion: How have modern readers, inside and outside Asia, reread the Buddhist texts to meet new questions of justice, science and equality?

story.title: The Refuges at Nagpur
story.kicker: On one October day in 1956, a huge crowd in central India repeats three short lines after a lawyer and statesman.
paragraphs: On October 14, 1956, an open ground in the city of Nagpur fills with people dressed in white. Estimates of the crowd vary, but most accounts say hundreds of thousands came. Most belong to communities then called untouchable, now often called Dalit. They have come to hear Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.

Ambedkar is one of the best-known people in India. Born into a Dalit family in 1891, he earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics. He chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution. For decades he fought caste discrimination. In 1935 he had said he was born a Hindu but would not die one.

That morning, Ambedkar and his wife take the Three Refuges and Five Precepts from the senior monk Chandramani. Then Ambedkar turns to the crowd and leads them in the refuges, the precepts and twenty-two vows of his own composition. The crowd repeats each line. In a few hours, one of the largest mass conversions in modern history has taken place.

Ambedkar died less than two months later. His book The Buddha and His Dhamma, published in 1957, reread the Buddhist texts as a charter of social equality. This chapter looks at Ambedkar and other modern readers: reformers, engaged Buddhists, scientists, women seeking ordination and environmentalists. Each reads old texts in a new light.
story.think: Why might a social reformer choose an ancient religious text as the ground for a movement for equality?

lessons.title: What Modernism Means
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars use 'Buddhist modernism' for movements since the 1800s that present Buddhism as rational, ethical and compatible with science.
reading: From the late 1800s, Asian and Western Buddhists began presenting their tradition in new ways. Colonial rule, Christian missions, printing and science all put pressure on older forms. Reformers answered by stressing meditation, ethics and reason, and by downplaying ritual, gods and miracles. Scholars call this broad pattern *Buddhist modernism*.

David McMahan's The Making of Buddhist Modernism (2008) traces its sources: European ideas about science and individual experience, Romantic ideas about nature and the self, and Asian reform movements. In Sri Lanka, Anagarika Dharmapala (1864 to 1933) led a Buddhist revival. He spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, as did the Japanese Zen teacher Soyen Shaku.

Modernism is not one school. It runs through Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike. Some scholars and traditional Buddhists caution that modernist readings can lose the devotion, ritual and cosmology that many Asian Buddhists hold central. Others see modernism as one more chapter in a long history of *adaptation*. Most scholars describe it rather than judge it.

words.d: movements since the 1800s that present Buddhism as rational, ethical and compatible with science
change that fits a tradition to a new time or place
a movement to renew a tradition's strength and practice
Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer (1864-1933) who spoke in Chicago in 1893

look.title: Two Presentations

look.prompt: Which features would a scholar call modernist? Why do scholars avoid calling either version the 'real' Buddhism?

lessons.title: Ambedkar's Buddhism
lessons.mainIdea: Ambedkar reread the Buddhist texts as a teaching of social equality, and his movement is today called Navayana by many followers.
reading: In The Buddha and His Dhamma (1957), Ambedkar retold the Buddha's life and teaching. He rejected parts of the tradition that he felt did not fit reason or justice. He questioned the traditional account of the Four Sights. He read suffering as including social suffering from poverty and caste. He stressed that the Buddha, as the texts present him, admitted people of every caste to the *sangha*.

His twenty-two vows set out a break with Hindu practice and a commitment to equality, reason and the precepts. Many of his followers call their tradition *Navayana*, the new vehicle, though the name is not used by all. They honor Ambedkar as Babasaheb and gather each year at Nagpur on the anniversary of the conversion.

Other Buddhists have responded in several ways. Some traditional scholars say Ambedkar departed from the texts on karma and rebirth. Many Dalit Buddhists see his work as recovering the texts' true social core. Scholars such as Christopher Queen treat his movement as a major example of socially engaged Buddhism. In India today, most Buddhists belong to communities shaped by his conversion.

words.d: the new vehicle: a name many followers use for Ambedkar's Buddhism
the name many people formerly called untouchable use for themselves in India
a hereditary social rank in South Asia
the community of monks and nuns, or of all Buddhists

lessons.title: Converts and Heritage Communities
lessons.mainIdea: In the United States, Asian heritage Buddhist communities and convert communities read and practice the texts in overlapping but different ways.
reading: American Buddhism is diverse. Many Buddhists in the United States belong to Asian heritage communities: Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai, Lao, Cambodian, Korean, Sri Lankan, Tibetan and more. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago, founded in 1944 by Rev. Gyomay Kubose, grew from a Japanese American Jodo Shinshu community after World War II.

Other American Buddhists are *converts*, people who came to Buddhism as adults, often through meditation centers, books or Zen and Tibetan teachers. Convert communities often stress meditation and read texts like the Satipatthana Sutta or the Heart Sutra closely. Heritage temples often center family ritual, festivals, chanting for the dead and language classes for children.

Scholars once described these as two Buddhisms, but many now call that too simple. Heritage communities include meditators; convert communities include ritual; children of immigrants and converts share centers. Some Asian American Buddhists have written about being overlooked when media present Buddhism as a white convert practice. A careful reader treats every community as an equal *interpreter* of the tradition.

words.d: a person who takes up a religion as an adult, not by birth
a religious community rooted in a family or cultural tradition passed down over generations
one who explains or lives out a text's meaning
True Pure Land Buddhism, a Japanese school centered on Amida Buddha

look.prompt: What does each community seem to value most in the texts? Describe without ranking.

lessons.title: Thich Nhat Hanh and Interbeing
lessons.mainIdea: Thich Nhat Hanh coined or popularized 'engaged Buddhism' during the Vietnam War, reading the texts as a call to act for peace.
reading: Thich Nhat Hanh (1926 to 2022) was a Vietnamese Zen monk. During the Vietnam War he worked for peace, trained young volunteers in relief work, and in 1966 founded the Order of Interbeing. He used the phrase *engaged Buddhism* for practice that responds to suffering in society, not only within the self. His 1967 book Vietnam: Lotus in a Sea of Fire made the case in English.

He read classic texts through this lens. His word interbeing, drawn from Huayan teaching, says that nothing exists by itself; a sheet of paper contains the cloud, the rain and the logger. His Five Mindfulness Trainings restate the five precepts in positive, social terms: protecting life, practicing generosity, responsible sexual conduct, loving speech and mindful consumption.

Martin Luther King Jr. nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1967. Exiled from Vietnam for decades, he built Plum Village in France, which drew practitioners from many countries. Some traditional critics said he changed the precepts too freely; his students answer that he kept their spirit. He remains one of the most read modern Buddhist teachers.

words.d: Buddhist practice that responds to social and political suffering
Thich Nhat Hanh's word for the dependence of every thing on every other thing
Thich Nhat Hanh's restatement of the five precepts in social terms

look.text: Thich Nhat Hanh writes that a poet will see a cloud floating in a sheet of paper: without the cloud, no rain; without rain, no trees; without trees, no paper. The paper 'inter-is' with the cloud.
look.cite: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding: Commentaries on the Prajnaparamita Heart Sutra (1988); paraphrased

check.why: Interbeing names the mutual dependence of all things.

check.why: King nominated him in 1967.

lessons.title: Saigon, 1963
lessons.mainIdea: The self-immolation of Thich Quang Duc in 1963, a protest against government policy toward Buddhists, drew a wide range of Buddhist and public responses.
reading: On June 11, 1963, the monk Thich Quang Duc sat down at a busy intersection in Saigon and set himself on fire. He was protesting the South Vietnamese government of Ngo Dinh Diem, which Buddhists said discriminated against them. Earlier that spring, government forces had fired on Buddhists in Hue during Vesak, killing several people.

A photograph by the journalist Malcolm Browne showed the monk sitting still in the flames. It spread around the world and put great pressure on the Diem government, which fell in a coup that November. Several other monks and nuns later died in the same way. The event is part of the history of *engaged Buddhism*, though it is not a model the tradition teaches.

Buddhists have responded in different ways. Thich Nhat Hanh, in a 1965 letter to Martin Luther King Jr., described the act as not suicide but an expression of will to be heard. Some Theravada and other teachers point to the precept against taking life and say they cannot approve. Many regard Thich Quang Duc with reverence. A careful student reports these views and the *context* without urging any view of the act.

words.d: setting oneself on fire, usually as a public protest
the events and conditions surrounding an act
Buddhist practice that responds to social and political suffering

look.title: Reading an Event
look.text: Fact: June 11, 1963, Saigon, a protest against government treatment of Buddhists. Response A: an act of compassion meant to move hearts. Response B: it conflicts with the first precept. Response C: reverence for the monk, whose heart, tradition says, did not burn.
look.prompt: Which Buddhist texts or ideas does each response draw on? Answer in the voice of a historian.

check.q: How did Thich Nhat Hanh describe the act in his 1965 letter?

check.why: His letter to King framed it as a cry to be heard.

check.q: Why do some teachers say they cannot approve of self-immolation?
choices: It is not in the Dhammapada

check.why: They point to the first precept.

lessons.title: The Dalai Lama and Science
lessons.mainIdea: The Fourteenth Dalai Lama has promoted dialogue with scientists and said Buddhist claims contradicted by science should be revised.
reading: Tenzin Gyatso, the Fourteenth *Dalai Lama*, was born in 1935 and has lived in exile in India since 1959. Tibetan Buddhists regard him as a manifestation of the bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989. Since 1987 he has met scientists in the Mind and Life dialogues on mind, meditation and the brain.

In The Universe in a Single Atom (2005), he wrote that if science proves a Buddhist claim wrong, Buddhists must accept the finding and give up the claim. He applied this to the traditional cosmology of a flat world with a central mountain, Meru, which he said can be set aside. He did not apply it to rebirth or consciousness, which he said science has not disproven.

His approach is a clear case of *modernist* reading from within a traditional lineage. Some scientists praise the dialogues as open inquiry. Some scholars ask whether meditation research strips practices from their religious setting. Some traditional Tibetan teachers keep the older cosmology in teaching. Each reader weighs text, lineage and evidence differently.

words.d: the title of a line of Tibetan teachers in the Gelug school; the Fourteenth is Tenzin Gyatso
the bodhisattva of compassion, whom Tibetan Buddhists believe the Dalai Lama embodies
belonging to Buddhist modernism: stressing reason, ethics and science
the central mountain of traditional Buddhist and Hindu cosmology

look.title: If Science Disagrees

look.prompt: Which claims did he say this applies to, and which did he say it does not yet touch? Why does the difference matter?

check.q: What question do some scholars raise about meditation research?
choices: Whether it strips practices from their religious setting

lessons.title: Nuns and Full Ordination
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya's account of the first nuns and the loss of the Theravada nuns' lineage frame a living debate over women's full ordination.
reading: The Vinaya, in the Cullavagga, tells how Mahapajapati Gotami, the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, asked to be ordained. The Buddha at first refused. Ananda asked whether women could reach awakening. The Buddha, as the text presents him, said yes, and allowed ordination with eight special rules, the *garudhammas*, that placed nuns under monks in certain ways.

The order of fully ordained Theravada nuns, bhikkhunis, died out in Sri Lanka around the eleventh century. The Vinaya requires both monks and nuns for a nun's ordination, so many Theravada authorities hold that the lineage cannot be revived. East Asian traditions kept their nuns' lineage, and in 1996 and 1998 Sri Lankan women were ordained with help from Korean and Taiwanese nuns.

Today the debate continues. Some Theravada monks, such as Ajahn Brahm in Australia in 2009, have supported ordinations and faced sanctions. Some traditional authorities reject them as invalid. Many women practice as ten-precept nuns without full ordination. Tibetan traditions have been discussing full ordination too. Scholars and practitioners read the same Vinaya passages to reach different *conclusions*.

words.d: a fully ordained Buddhist nun
the eight special rules the Vinaya says were given for nuns
the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, the first nun in Vinaya tradition
a judgment reached by reasoning from evidence

lessons.title: Readings for the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist environmentalists read texts on interdependence, the precepts and the forest life as grounds for protecting nature.
reading: Beginning in the late 1980s, some Thai monks wrapped trees in orange robes and ordained them, so that cutting them would be seen as harming a monk. Scholars such as Susan Darlington call them *ecology monks*. They drew on the forest settings of the Buddha's life, the precept against taking life, and the respect owed to the robe.

Other readers draw on the texts directly. Dhammapada 49 compares the sage to a bee who takes nectar without harming the flower's color or scent. Thai reformer Sulak Sivaraksa and American writer Joanna Macy read dependent arising as teaching that humans and nature are bound together. Thich Nhat Hanh wrote of the earth as a living mother.

Some scholars caution that early texts were not written with modern ecology in mind. The suttas describe forests as places of practice and sometimes of danger, and rules against harming plants belong to monastic discipline. Environmental Buddhists answer that each generation applies the texts to its own suffering. Both points belong in a careful account of *eco-Buddhism*.

words.d: Thai monks who use Buddhist ritual, such as tree ordination, to protect forests
Buddhist readings and movements that apply teachings to protecting nature
the idea that all things depend on one another; related to dependent arising

lessons.title: Inside and Outside
lessons.mainIdea: Modern readers include monks, lay teachers, reformers, converts and academic scholars, and each brings different aims to the texts.
reading: Who counts as a reader of the Buddhist texts? Monks and nuns who chant them daily. Laypeople who hear them at funerals. Reformers like Ambedkar. Teachers like Thich Nhat Hanh. Scientists in dialogue with the Dalai Lama. And academic scholars, many of whom are not Buddhist, who study the texts historically.

Religious studies scholars sometimes speak of *insider* and *outsider* readers. An insider reads the text as part of their own practice and community. An outsider reads it from a distance, asking historical or comparative questions. Many people are both: a Buddhist scholar, or a non-Buddhist who has practiced for years. The terms describe stances more than people.

Each stance sees things the other can miss. Insiders know how a text lives: what is chanted, when, and why it moves people. Outsiders may notice change over time and parallels in other traditions. This course takes an outsider's descriptive stance while treating insider readings as authoritative for their communities. That is not a ranking. It is a method.

words.d: a reader who approaches a text as part of their own religious practice
a reader who studies a text from outside the practicing community
the position from which a reader approaches a text

look.text: A Sri Lankan monk chants verse 5 at a peace ceremony. A historian notes it has parallels in the Gandhari Dharmapada. A Dalit activist in Nagpur quotes it at a rally against caste violence.
look.prompt: What does each reader's stance let them see? What might each miss?

check.q: What is an insider reader?
choices: One who reads a text as part of their own practice
check.why: Insiders read from within a practicing community.

check.q: What stance does this course take?
choices: An insider stance that teaches practice
A descriptive outsider stance that respects insider readings

check.q: Why do scholars say insider and outsider describe stances more than people?

lessons.title: Reading Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: A careful student can compare modern readings by asking what text each uses, what question it answers and whom it serves, without ranking them.
reading: This chapter has met many modern readings. Ambedkar read the texts for social equality. Thich Nhat Hanh read them for peace and interbeing. The Dalai Lama read them in dialogue with science. Women seeking ordination read the Vinaya for precedent. Ecology monks read them for the earth. Each is a real *interpretation*.

One way to compare without ranking uses three questions. What passages does the reader cite? What question from their own time are they answering? Which community do they speak for and to? These questions turn opinions into evidence. They let a student explain why readers differ instead of simply declaring a winner.

Traditional readers raise a fourth question: does the reading stay faithful to the texts and the lineage? Modern readers often answer that faithfulness means applying the Dhamma to present suffering. That debate itself is part of the tradition. A careful student can report it, weigh the evidence each side gives, and still leave the verdict to the communities themselves.

words.d: a reader's account of what a text means
an earlier case used to guide a later decision
staying true to a text's words or a tradition's teaching
